verified_ref: Taittiriya Upanishad 3.6.1 (Bhriguvalli, anuvaka 6, opening sentences); same in Mahadeva Sastri's edition and Muller SBE 15 (Taitt. III.6).
attribution_note: No speaker in the text; the Upanishad narrates Bhrigu's conclusion. 'Narrator' is right.
translation_note: 'Joy' for anandah is acceptable, but classical translators use 'bliss', and the commentators insist it is not ordinary pleasure. The excerpt stops before the anuvaka's final line (the knower becomes rich in food, offspring and fame), which is fine.
context: Bhrigu asks his father Varuna to teach him Brahman. Varuna gives only a test (that from which beings are born, by which they live, into which they return) and tells him to seek it through tapas. Bhrigu proposes food, breath, mind and understanding, returning each time; on the fifth inquiry he sees that bliss fits. The text then calls this the wisdom of Bhrigu and Varuna, and the next anuvaka turns to reverence for food.

key_terms.sense: he came to understand that bliss is Brahman
disciplined, concentrated reflection; the only method Varuna gives
rooted in the highest space; Shankara reads it as the space within the heart
becomes firmly grounded
the knowledge Bhrigu learned and Varuna taught

core_teaching: The source, support and end of all beings is bliss, meaning a non-dual fullness at the core of the self, not a passing pleasure. It is found by going inward layer by layer through patient, concentrated reflection.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), in A. Mahadeva Sastri's 1903 translation
commentaries.gist: With a mind purified by tapas, Bhrigu saw that breath, mind and understanding fell short, went inward step by step, and found bliss, the innermost, to be Brahman. So composure of the outer and inner senses is the means.

commentaries.who: Sureshvara, Vartika on Shankara's bhashya (Advaita)
commentaries.gist: The knower sets aside all five sheaths and rests in the support that lies beyond cause and effect. The 'highest space' is the self, where the distinction between 'I' and 'you' falls away.

commentaries.who: Unmarked commentary passage in Mahadeva Sastri's edition (which translates Shankara and Sayana)
commentaries.gist: Small pleasures are mixed with pain: the effort to get them, comparison with greater ones, and their loss. The bliss meant here is glimpsed in deep sleep and absorption, and is more than the mere absence of pain.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to look beneath achievements and comforts for a quieter gladness that is already there. It is also a model of learning by repeated honest reflection rather than borrowed answers, and of a parent who gives clues instead of conclusions.
misreadings: Not 'life is about having fun': the commentators set this bliss against ordinary pleasures
Not an instruction to feel happy; it describes the ground of being, not a mood
'Entering joy at death' is a statement about the source of beings, not a promise about how dying feels
cautions: Mentions death ('into joy they enter'), which may sting for the recently bereaved
For a low reader, 'everything is born of joy' can feel invalidating; present it as something uncovered slowly, as Bhrigu did
speaks_to: parents or teachers who guide by questions
not_for: fresh grief
a reader being told to 'just be positive'
research_note: The edition marks Sureshvara (S) and Anandagiri (A) explicitly; some unmarked paragraphs could be Shankara or Sayana, so I attributed only what I could identify.

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 2.16.8 (Mumukshu-vyavahara prakarana, sarga 16, on good company). Verse and number confirmed in the Nirnaya Sagar text printed with Anandabodhendra's Tatparya-prakasha (Pansikar ed., 1937 scan); Mitra 1891, Mumukshu ch. XVI para 8.
attribution_note: Vasishtha to Rama, as stated.
translation_note: 'Good company' (sadhu-sangati) means the company of the wise and virtuous (sadhus), not friends in general. Anandabodhendra glosses 'not even a little' as 'not even for a moment'.
context: After chapters on calm, inquiry and contentment, Vasishtha describes the fourth gatekeeper of freedom: the company of the wise. Just before this verse he says such company makes solitude feel like companionship, turns hardship into ease and grows discernment. Just after, he calls it a lamp on the right path. He ends by saying that practising any one of the four gatekeepers brings the others.

key_terms.sense: association with good, wise people
the hardest circumstances
by those who have become helpless or powerless
must not be given up, even slightly

core_teaching: However bad things get, and however powerless you feel, keep some contact with wise and good people. It is one of four entry points (with calm, inquiry and contentment) to freedom, and any one of them strengthens the others.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary on the Yoga Vasishtha)
commentaries.gist: Introduces the chapter as the fourth gatekeeper and adds that serving even one of the four bears fruit. Glosses 'not even a little' as not even for a moment.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Mumukshu ch. XVI)
commentaries.gist: The surrounding verses say wise company clears inner darkness, heals mental ills, eases the pain of poverty and death, and is worth more than pilgrimage, gifts or austerities.

practical_reading: In low times people tend to withdraw. Teachers read this as: keep at least one thread to someone who steadies you (a mentor, a satsang, a wise friend), even for a few minutes.
misreadings: Not 'only keep positive people around you' or drop friends who are struggling
Not a demand to socialise when depleted; brief contact counts
'Good company' means wise and decent people, not just any crowd
cautions: Nearby verses say wise company makes death feel like a festival (16.3) and that those who neglect it are fuel for hell (16.16); do not quote these to someone grieving
Where the 'company' is the source of harm, steer towards safe, chosen people
not_for: someone whose circle is harming them
a socially anxious reader pressured to perform
research_note: The Yoga Vasishtha has one classical commentary (Anandabodhendra); its glosses here are brief. Mitra's 1891 translation is loose but confirms the verse position.

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 5.22.34 (Upashama prakarana, sarga 22, start of the Bali story). Confirmed in the Nirnaya Sagar text with Tatparya-prakasha; Mitra, Upasama ch. XXII para 34.
attribution_note: Bali reflecting to himself. Anandabodhendra places him at the window of a jewelled mansion on a peak of Meru, so 'by his window' is right.
translation_note: vidambana is farce or mockery. Anandabodhendra: for a wise heart this repetition is like re-doing what is already done, something to laugh at. Mitra's 'chewing the chewed' is his own gloss.
context: Vasishtha tells Rama the story of Bali, who has ruled for ages. Sated, Bali asks what use his sovereignty and fading pleasures are: the same bathing, eating and sleeping, actions rising and falling like waves. He asks what deed would leave nothing further to do. He then remembers asking his father Virochana about the final state and Virochana's parable of the king and his minister, the mind, and he calls his teacher Shukra for instruction.

key_terms.sense: again and again
an endless chain of tasks
a discerning, thoughtful person
mockery, farce

core_teaching: Repeating the same pleasures and duties without any aim that ends the need for more looks absurd to a thoughtful mind. That disenchantment opens the inquiry; it is not the conclusion.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: The daily round brings nothing new, so craving for it is cause for shame. Bali is looking for an aim that, once gained, leaves nothing more to do, and he sees none in pleasure.

commentaries.who: Context of the story (Mitra tr., Upasama chs. XXII-XXVI)
commentaries.gist: Bali's weariness leads him to recall Virochana's teaching that mastering the mind, the minister, wins everything, and he seeks Shukra's guidance. The answer is inner mastery, not escape.

practical_reading: Treat the 'same day again' feeling as a prompt to ask what your days are for, not as a verdict that they are worthless. Bali's next step is to look for teaching, not to walk away.
misreadings: Not advice to quit your work or duties
Not proof that life is meaningless; the story goes on to an answer
Not contempt for people whose work is routine
cautions: Used alone it can deepen hopelessness in burnout or depression; pair it with the story's resolution, as our misuse note says
The chapter mentions repeated births
not_for: a reader who already feels worthless
depression, unless the follow-up verse comes with it

verified_ref: Mundaka Upanishad 3.1.4 (same numbering in Shankara's and Madhva's commentaries).
attribution_note: The Upanishad's frame is Angiras teaching Shaunaka.
translation_note: Two loose spots. (1) 'Does not talk over others' and the line 'the wise stop arguing' are modern glosses of na ativadi. Shankara: he does not talk of anything other than the Self. Madhva (Vasu tr.): he no longer claims 'I am the doer' and gives up useless controversy. Suggest 'is not a man of many words' or 'has no need to out-talk anyone'. (2) 'Yet active': Shankara says the activity is knowledge, meditation and dispassion, and rejects reading it as ritual or worldly work. Madhva reads it as worship, duties and teaching. 'Stay fully active' fits Madhva, not Shankara.
context: This follows the two-birds image (3.1.1-3): the one who sees the radiant Lord is freed from grief and becomes stainless. This verse describes how such a knower lives. The next verse (3.1.5) says the Self is reached through truth, austerity, right knowledge and self-control.

key_terms.sense: this is the life (Shankara: the Lord, the life of life) shining in all beings
not one who talks beyond or over (see translation note)
one whose play and delight are in the Self
active; the commentators disagree on what the activity is
the best among the knowers of Brahman

core_teaching: One who sees the one Self shining in all beings finds delight within, has nothing to prove in argument, and remains engaged. The commentators disagree about what that engagement is.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita)
commentaries.gist: Seeing only the Self everywhere, the knower has nothing else to talk about. 'Active' means knowledge, meditation and freedom from desire. Mixing ritual work with knowledge is rejected, because outer activity and inner delight conflict.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), Srisa Chandra Vasu tr.
commentaries.gist: Seeing that the Lord is the real doer, the knower stops boasting 'I act'. He contemplates the Lord's play, and when not absorbed he stays active in worship and duties and teaches seekers.

practical_reading: A joy that does not depend on winning arguments or outside props, together with steady engagement in one's own work, without the need to dominate.
misreadings: Not 'avoid all disagreement'; conflict avoidance is not the point
For Shankara 'active' does not mean hustle; for Madhva it means service and worship
'Delight in the Self' is not self-absorption
cautions: On a 'running on empty' day, 'active' should not be heard as 'do more'
speaks_to: needing an inner source of joy
people worn out by constant argument
not_for: someone who needs to speak up, for example about abuse; do not read it as 'stay quiet'

verified_ref: Isha Upanishad, mantra 2 (same in Shankara's and Madhva's editions).
translation_note: 'In this spirit' (evam) is a common modern reading that links it to verse 1's renunciation. Shankara reads evam as 'in this way, by performing prescribed rites'. Madhva reads the doing as 'without desire for fruit'. Both fit the English loosely.
context: Verse 1 says everything is pervaded by the Lord: enjoy by letting go and covet no one's wealth. Verse 2 speaks to those who want to live out a full life. Verse 3 warns that those who destroy their own self go to sunless worlds.

key_terms.sense: only by doing
works; Shankara: rites such as the agnihotra
may wish to live a hundred years
action does not cling to (stain) the person

core_teaching: A full life of work is compatible with inner freedom if action is done in the right spirit. The commentators differ on what that spirit is.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), S. Sitarama Sastri tr.
commentaries.gist: Verse 1 is for those able to renounce. This verse is for those who want a full life and cannot renounce: for them, doing the enjoined rites is the only way bad karma won't stick. Renunciation remains the higher path.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), Srisa Chandra Vasu tr. 1909
commentaries.gist: 'Doing' means acting without desire for results while worshipping the Lord. Neglecting this is a fault even for the wise, so everyone should keep working. Verse 1 teaches detachment; verse 2 adds that action must go with it.

practical_reading: Keep doing your work wholeheartedly, for a long life, but loosen your grip on outcomes so the work does not stick to you.
misreadings: Not a call to overwork
Not a promise of a long life
Shankara does not treat this as the highest path; don't present it as the Upanishad's last word on action versus renunciation
cautions: On a 'running on empty' action day, frame it as working without clinging, not 'keep pushing'
'A hundred years' may sting for someone seriously ill
not_for: a reader facing terminal illness

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 5.66.34-35 (Upashama prakarana, sarga 66, in the story of Bhasa and Vilasa). Confirmed in the Nirnaya Sagar text with Tatparya-prakasha (v.34 numbered, v.35 glossed); Mitra vol. III, Upasama ch. LXVI paras 34-35 (the story begins in ch. LXV).
attribution_note: Bhasa answering Vilasa. The colophon calls the chapter the 'teaching on impermanence' within the Bhasa-Vilasa story.
translation_note: Mitra's rendering agrees in substance (the mind flutters between what it has done, is doing and will do, caught in its own fancies).
context: Vasishtha tells of two boys raised in sage Atri's hermitage on Mount Sahya. When their fathers die they mourn, then spend long years apart in austerities without gaining knowledge. Meeting again as old men, Vilasa asks if Bhasa is at peace. Bhasa answers that no one rests while desire and fear remain, and describes life's stream of duties and the spinning mind. In the next chapter both turn to self-knowledge and become free while living.

key_terms.sense: great waves of tasks
rest, repose
set dancing by worry
a net of reckonings and calculations
the bird of the mind faints (commentary: is stupefied)

core_teaching: A mind swept along by endless tasks and the 'done, doing, still to do' reckoning never rests. Rest comes from understanding, not from more effort or harder austerity.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: The 'bird of the mind', bound in the net of reckonings, is stupefied. Around it he explains the river of activity running through every birth, and the body as the precious instrument for life's highest aim.

commentaries.who: Context of the story (Mitra tr., Upasama chs. LXV-LXVII)
commentaries.gist: Years of grief and hard austerity without understanding left both friends restless. Their honest exchange turns them to self-knowledge, and they are freed while still living.

practical_reading: Notice the to-do loop running in the background. The answer the story gives is not a better list but stepping back to understand what the mind is doing.
misreadings: Not 'stop doing your tasks'
Not that hard work is pointless; the story's point is effort without understanding
cautions: The story opens with the death of both fathers and long mourning; useful but tender for the bereaved
For a parent of small children, don't imply the busyness is a personal failing
not_for: someone in crisis who needs practical help more than reflection

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 5.11.6 (Upashama prakarana, sarga 11, Janaka's address to his mind). Confirmed in the Nirnaya Sagar text with Tatparya-prakasha; Mitra, Upasama ch. XI para 6.
attribution_note: Janaka speaking to his own mind at night after the day's duties, as stated.
translation_note: chinta can mean 'thinking' as much as 'worrying'; v.8 speaks of a 'net of thoughts' (chinta-jala). 'Worrying' is defensible. samsara is the round of worldly existence, and 'world of troubles' is an interpretive gloss.
context: Janaka has overheard the sages' songs and reflected. He rises to do the day's work without clinging and, after the day's duties, speaks to his mind at night. V.5: restless mind, the world does not make you happy; calm does. V.6 is this verse. V.7: like a watered tree putting out a hundred branches, desire makes you endlessly needy. V.8: births and worldly troubles grow from this net of thoughts, so drop it and turn to calm.

key_terms.sense: floods of alternatives and imaginings
you conjure them up casually, as if in play
swelling, expansion
thinking, anxious thought
calming, quieting

core_teaching: The troubled world we live in is largely built and enlarged by our own unchecked imagining; quieting that habit shrinks it.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: Glosses calm (v.5) as an undistracted state whose essence is the self's own happiness. Desire (v.7) leaves one with endless needs, and births and worldly troubles grow from the net of thoughts about objects (v.8).

commentaries.who: Context of the episode (Mitra tr., Upasama chs. IX-XI)
commentaries.gist: Janaka does not renounce his kingdom: he does the day's duties without a sense of doership, then at night gently counsels his restless mind.

practical_reading: Notice when you are spinning 'what if' scenarios. Each one adds weight; come back to the task in front of you.
misreadings: Not a claim that worries are imaginary or that real risks are not real
Not a call to stop planning
cautions: For 'work feels unsafe', don't imply the danger is all in the reader's head; real threats need real action
For 'far from parents', worry about ageing parents is a form of love; acknowledge that
not_for: someone facing real danger or abuse who needs to act

verified_ref: Vishnu Gita, ch. 1 (Vairagya-yoga), in the gods' hymn to Vishnu. Numbered 1.63 in the 1919 Bharat Dharma Mahamandal edition (Benares, Sanskrit with Hindi), which counts speaker lines such as 'Suta uvaca' and 'Vyasa uvaca' as verses. Our 1.60 probably follows a text without those numbers; the wording matches.
attribution_note: Speaker and listener (the gods to Vishnu) are right; within the text, Vyasa narrates to Suta. CAUTION on the text itself: this is not a classical Purana passage. The earliest edition we found is the Shri Bharat Dharma Mahamandal's (Benares, 1919). It is one of five sectarian 'Gitas' (Vishnu, Surya, Shakti, Dhisha, Shambhu) the Mahamandal published around 1919-20. Its own preface, printed in the 1920 Shambhu Gita, says the five were obtained through its research department and had never been properly published. Historian Malavika Kasturi (2015) documents the Mahamandal promoting these five Gitas. We found no independent manuscript tradition and no classical commentary. Present it as an early-20th-century devotional text.
translation_note: moha-jam bhayam is fear born of delusion or confusion; the edition's Hindi says the same.
context: Suta asks Vyasa how the Lord once freed the gods from fear. Vyasa explains that creation is a play of opposites in which gods and anti-gods alternate in power. The frightened gods praise Vishnu: they move only by his power, forget him through maya, and he cures their delusion through adversity, which they call his compassion. Then comes this verse, and they ask to be taught so they never fall into delusion again. Vishnu replies that they slipped from right conduct and forgot their duty, which is why fear seized them, and he teaches dispassion.

key_terms.sense: we have come for refuge
you who are tender to those who seek shelter
fear born of delusion or confusion
is destroyed, goes away

core_teaching: Fear rooted in confusion can be dissolved by turning for shelter and asking to understand. The gods ask not only for rescue but to be taught, so the confusion does not return.

commentaries.who: Hindi translation in the Mahamandal edition (1919; no classical commentary exists)
commentaries.gist: Renders the gods' plea: we seek refuge in you, lover of those who seek shelter; act so that our delusion-born fear is destroyed. The next verse asks for teaching so they never fall into delusion again.

commentaries.who: Context of the hymn (Sanskrit text, Vishnu Gita ch. 1, vv. 60-70 in the 1919 numbering)
commentaries.gist: The gods say they move only by Vishnu's power yet forget him through maya, and he cures this through adversity, which they call his mercy. Vishnu replies that they lapsed from right conduct and forgot their duty, hence the fear.

practical_reading: Saying plainly 'I'm afraid and I need help making sense of this' is a legitimate first step. Ask for clarity, not just relief.
misreadings: Not 'your fear is your own fault'. Vishnu's reply in the text does tie the gods' fear to their own lapse, but do not import that onto a reader facing real danger at work
Not passivity: the gods go on to ask for teaching
cautions: A late text: label it accurately
The hymn's idea that adversity is the Lord's corrective (v.62 in the 1919 edition) can feel like blame to someone being harmed
not_for: someone who needs practical safety steps, such as harassment at work, unless paired with action
research_note: No classical commentary exists. The two commentary items are the 1919 edition's own Hindi rendering and the surrounding Sanskrit text, read in the archive.org OCR.

verified_ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 1.4.14 (Kanva recension; Madhavananda's numbering; Muller SBE 15 I.4.14). The wisdomlib Devanagari prints the verse number as 15, but the transliteration and translation number it 14.
attribution_note: No speaker; part of the Upanishad's creation account.
translation_note: 'As with the help of a king' follows the reading Madhavananda attributes to Sureshvara's Vartika ('as one does through the king'). Shankara's own reading pictures a householder contending even with the king. 'Power over power' renders kshatrasya kshatram (Madhavananda: 'controller of the Kshatriya').
context: Brahman, alone, did not flourish. It projected ruling power (the warrior gods such as Indra and Varuna), then the wealth-producing gods, then the nourisher Pushan, and still did not flourish, so it projected dharma. The next verse (1.4.15) names these as the four varnas and warns that one who dies without knowing the Self is not protected by it.

key_terms.sense: what is right, the law (Madhavananda: righteousness)
the power over power, the controller of rulers
the weaker hopes to prevail over the stronger
truth

core_teaching: What is right stands above raw power. Through it the weak can prevail over the strong, and what is right in practice is the same as what is true.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), Madhavananda tr.
commentaries.gist: Dharma was created to restrain even the fierce ruling class, so it controls everyone. A weak person can overcome a stronger one by its strength. As conduct it is called righteousness, as knowledge truth; they are one.

commentaries.who: Sureshvara, Vartika (as cited in Madhavananda's note)
commentaries.gist: The more obvious sense of the simile is that the weak prevail as one does with the backing of the king.

commentaries.who: Swami Krishnananda (Divine Life Society), commentary on the Brihadaranyaka
commentaries.gist: Dharma is the invisible ordering law, the ruler of rulers, which binds even the lawmaker. Strength and weakness depend on one's alignment with it, and truth and righteousness are two sides of one coin.

practical_reading: When you are outmatched, anchor yourself in what is fair and true and in legitimate structures, rather than trying to match force with force.
misreadings: Not a promise that the right side always wins quickly
Not a licence for vigilante 'justice'
Shankara ties dharma here to caste duties; don't present it as a modern human-rights doctrine without saying that is an application
cautions: The surrounding verses (1.4.11-15) describe the creation of the four varnas, and Shankara's commentary links dharma to caste duty; avoid quoting context that reads as endorsing caste hierarchy
For someone being hurt by a person close to them, add practical safety advice; 'dharma will protect you' should not replace seeking help
speaks_to: standing up to someone who hurt you
not_for: someone in immediate danger who needs practical steps first

verified_ref: Ashtavakra Gita 16.3. Same number in the GRETIL text (data entry by John Richards), Swami Nityaswarupananda's Ashtavakra Samhita and Lala Baijnath's translation (archive.org item dated 1904).
attribution_note: Traditionally ascribed to the sage Ashtavakra instructing King Janaka; I did not research its date. Chapter 16 is titled 'Special instruction' (Nityaswarupananda; Baijnath: 'Eleven verses on special instruction'). Numbering is stable across the editions checked.
translation_note: ayasa means exertion or straining. Baijnath: all exertion causes pain, though no one knows it.
context: 16.1: you can recite and hear many scriptures, but you will not be at ease without forgetting everything. 16.2: enjoy, work or meditate, and your mind will still long for what lies beyond all desire. 16.3 is this verse. 16.4: only the 'master idler', to whom even blinking is a strain, is happy. 16.5: freed from 'this is done, that is not', the mind no longer cares about the four aims of life.

key_terms.sense: exertion, straining
miserable, suffering
teaching, instruction
peace, release
the fortunate, blessed one

core_teaching: Suffering comes from the strain of desire-driven striving. Seeing this clearly is itself the teaching that frees.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Ashtavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama) notes
commentaries.gist: All exertion presupposes a desire for something not yet had; satisfied desire breeds more desire, unsatisfied desire hurts. Uprooting desire makes one inwardly inactive, though outwardly one may still act.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Lala Baijnath, The Ashtavakra Gita (translation with brief notes)
commentaries.gist: Renders it as: every exertion brings pain though no one recognises it, and whoever takes this single lesson to heart finds peace. His note on 16.1 says the last word of this teaching is silence.

practical_reading: Notice the extra layer of strain (gripping, urgency, needing a particular outcome) on top of what you are doing, and release that even while you keep doing the work.
misreadings: Not against effort or responsibility; Nityaswarupananda says outward activity may continue
Not 'parenting should feel effortless'
The next verse's 'master idler' means inner non-grasping, not laziness
cautions: If 16.4 is quoted, explain it; for a tired parent 'master idler' can sound like a dig
not_for: someone already unable to get started, who may hear it as permission to give up
research_note: No traditional Sanskrit commentary was available to me; I used two modern translations with notes.

verified_ref: Aitareya Upanishad 2.1.3 (= GRETIL 'aitup 2.3'; = Aitareya Aranyaka II.5.1, Müller SBE 1, paras 6-9). Our Sanskrit is the second half of 2.1.3.
attribution_note: No named speaker; 'Seer' / narrator is fine.
translation_note: Fair. 'He' is the father. Shankara reads 'janmano 'gre 'dhi' as right after birth (through the birth rites); Müller, following Sayana, as both before and just after birth. 'Second birth' in the text is the father's own self emerging from the mother's womb as the son; our line 'through them you are born a second time' is a fair modern gloss. Note the original speaks of a son (kumara).
context: Chapter 2 of the Aitareya describes three births of a person: as seed in the father, passed to the mother (first); as the child born and raised (second); and, after the father hands his duties to the son and dies, as rebirth (third). Just before this, the mother nourishes the unborn child and is to be nourished in turn. Just after, the son takes the father's place in good works and the father, his work done, departs. The chapter ends with the sage Vamadeva, who saw through all these births while still in the womb.

key_terms.sense: raises, nurtures the child
in that he nurtures his own self
for the continuity of these worlds (generations)
second birth

core_teaching: In raising a child a parent nurtures a continuation of their own self, and that is how the generations carry on. Shankara adds that this keeps the world going but is not itself the path to liberation.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), Aitareya bhashya (Sanskrit, GRETIL)
commentaries.gist: The father nurtures the newborn through birth rites; the father's self is born as the son, so caring for the son is caring for himself. This is done to keep the worlds continuing, not for liberation.

commentaries.who: Max Müller tr., Aitareya Aranyaka II.5 (SBE 1, 1879), with Sayana's reading
commentaries.gist: Translates the father as raising the child before and right after birth, which is raising his own self; this is the second birth. Notes that some manuscripts open the chapter by asking pregnant women to leave.

practical_reading: Parenting is not only giving; it shapes the parent too, and continues something of you. Seen that way, the daily care is also self-care and legacy.
misreadings: Not 'your child is an extension of you to be shaped as you like'
Not a claim that only sons carry on the family, even though the original speaks of a son
cautions: The chapter's frame is the cycle of rebirth, and the next sentence is about the parent dying (third birth); don't quote further
The original is father- and son-centred; keep the reading gender-neutral
Can sting for parents of a child who has died, adoptive parents, or people unable to have children
not_for: bereaved parents
people struggling with infertility

verified_ref: Shambhu Gita, ch. 4 ('Devaloka-nirupana', Sadashiva and the Pitris), verse 85 in the Mahamandal edition (1920 printing; same number in the 1989 second edition). That edition counts speaker lines ('pitara ucuh' etc.) as verses; our 4.83 probably follows a text that doesn't. Wording matches.
attribution_note: Shiva (Sadashiva) to the Pitris, correct. This is one of the five sectarian 'Gitas' (Vishnu, Shambhu, Shakti, Surya, Dhisha) published by the Shri Bharat Dharma Mahamandal, Benares, c. 1916-1920; no independent manuscript tradition or classical commentary found (see vishnu_gita.1.60 entry). Present it as an early-20th-century devotional text, not an ancient one.
translation_note: Two problems. (1) 'jnani-sannidhau' does not mean the effort is 'made in the company of the wise'; the edition's own Hindi renders the point as how the effort 'is regarded' (by the wise), i.e. 'in the judgement of the wise'. (2) The verse is half a sentence: 'is the better one' comes from the next verse (86), which says such effort brings more welfare to people than punishment. Suggest: 'But the effort by which people never come to deserve punishment at all is, in the eyes of the wise, the greater good.'
context: Shiva describes to the ancestors the four divisions of the earthly sphere (the ancestors' world, the human world, the world of ghosts and hell) and says Dharmaraja's (Yama's) rule extends over them. If the ancestors make firm daily effort, he says, they can help keep creation in balance without needing Yama's rod. Making people righteous through punishment is good, but effort that keeps them from ever deserving punishment does more for their welfare (vv. 84-86).

key_terms.sense: the rod: punishment, coercive discipline
deserving punishment
effort, deliberate care
in the view (literally, presence) of the wise

core_teaching: Preventing wrongdoing through guidance is better than correcting it through punishment. The context is cosmic governance by the ancestors, not parenting.

commentaries.who: Hindi translation in the Mahamandal edition (1920; no classical commentary exists)
commentaries.gist: Renders vv. 80-86: with firm effort the ancestors can protect creation's harmony without Yama's punishment; making people dharmic by punishment is good, but effort so they never deserve it is considered more beneficial.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Sanskrit text, Shambhu Gita ch. 4)
commentaries.gist: The chapter, framed as Shiva answering the Pitris, maps the worlds and assigns the ancestors a protective role over human welfare; this verse states the preventive ideal within that role.

practical_reading: For a parent, the analogy is: put more energy into setting a child up to do well (routines, example, explanation) than into consequences after the fact. Punishment isn't rejected, just ranked lower.
misreadings: Not a scriptural verdict against all discipline; the previous verse calls punishment-based effort good
Not about parenting in the original; it is an analogy, so don't present it as 'Shiva's parenting advice'
cautions: Late text; label accurately
Surrounding verses discuss hell and ghost-realms; avoid quoting them
speaks_to: parents who feel they are always correcting
not_for: a parent dealing with a child's serious harm to others, where it could read as 'never set consequences'
research_note: No commentary exists; both items are the edition's own Hindi rendering and the surrounding text. Prasang is null in our data.

verified_ref: Aitareya Upanishad 2.1.2 to the first half of 2.1.3 (GRETIL 'aitup 2.2-2.3'; Aitareya Aranyaka II.5.1, Müller SBE 1, paras 4-6).
attribution_note: No named speaker; narrator is fine.
translation_note: Accurate. 'It' is the father's seed; Shankara says it becomes part of the mother like her own limb, so it does not harm her as a foreign growth would. 'This self of his' = the husband's self in the unborn child. Shankara names who must nourish the nourisher: her husband.
context: The Aitareya's account of three births. The first is the seed passing from father to mother. Here the unborn child becomes part of the mother, she nourishes it, and she in turn must be cared for. Then she carries the child and the father takes up its care from birth. That care is the second birth; the third comes after the parent's death.

key_terms.sense: becomes one with her own self
does not harm (her)
she who nourishes, causes to grow
is to be nourished, cared for

core_teaching: The mother nourishes the child within her, and so she must herself be nourished and protected; care has to flow back to the carer.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), Aitareya bhashya (Sanskrit, GRETIL)
commentaries.gist: The pregnant woman nourishes the husband's self within her by avoiding harmful food and eating well; so she must be nourished and protected by her husband, since no bond in the world lasts without help given in return.

commentaries.who: Max Müller tr., Aitareya Aranyaka II.5 (SBE 1, 1879)
commentaries.gist: Renders it plainly: she nourishes her husband's self, the son, within her; she who nourishes is to be nourished; she bears the germ, and he raises the child before and after birth.

practical_reading: Whoever is doing most of the caring, whether mother, father or another carer, needs to be cared for too. Ask for help, or offer it, today.
misreadings: Not 'the mother's role is only to carry the father's child'
Not limited to pregnancy; teachers apply the principle to any carer
cautions: Describes conception and pregnancy; sensitive for readers with pregnancy loss or infertility
Frames the child as the husband's self; keep the reading inclusive of single parents and other family shapes
Müller notes some manuscripts open this chapter by asking pregnant women to leave; worth knowing, not quoting
not_for: someone grieving a pregnancy loss

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 1.16.22 (Vairagya-prakarana, sarga 16, 'the wickedness of the mind'). Confirmed in the Nirnaya Sagar text with Anandabodhendra's Tatparya-prakasha (Pansikar ed., 1937); Mitra 1891, Vairagya ch. XVI v. 22.
attribution_note: Rama speaking to Vishvamitra and Vasishtha in Dasharatha's court, as stated.
translation_note: Fair. Anandabodhendra reads 'karyeshu' as sense objects (the mind clings to them at once) and the second half as: it quits even long-practised good pursuits, the way a child drops his lessons the moment he gets a toy. So the child is abandoning work FOR the toy, not tiring of the toy. Mitra (1891) reads the half-line differently again. Our 'loses interest like a child with a toy' is a defensible plain reading; the commentator's version (dropping the real task for a distraction) fits a 'can't get started' plan even better.
context: Rama, asked why he has grown so withdrawn, gives a long lament. This chapter is about the mind: he says it is hotter than fire, harder to master than a mountain is to cross and tougher than a thunderbolt (v.21). After this verse he compares it to a sea full of whirlpools, says subduing it is harder than drinking the ocean or uprooting Meru, and that it is the root of all trouble and must be treated like an illness.

key_terms.sense: the mind swoops, falls upon
like a bird upon pieces of meat
in a moment it turns away, gives up
as a child with (or because of) a toy

core_teaching: The untrained mind grabs at whatever attracts it and then abandons it, including worthwhile work, almost at once. Rama is naming the problem honestly; Vasishtha's later teaching is that the mind can be trained.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (Sanskrit commentary)
commentaries.gist: The mind attaches instantly to sense objects and just as quickly abandons even long-practised good activities, like a boy who drops his long-pursued studies the moment he is handed some toy.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Vairagya ch. XVI)
commentaries.gist: Surrounding verses call the mind restless and dull at once, harder to subdue than drinking the ocean, the cause of every exertion, and something to be treated like a disease; Rama asks how to master it.

practical_reading: Starting and dropping tasks is an old, ordinary feature of the mind, not a personal defect. Naming the pattern is the first step; the YV's own answer is patient, repeated training rather than self-blame.
misreadings: Not a diagnosis that you are lazy or broken
Not a claim that the mind can't be trained: it is Rama's complaint, which the rest of the book answers
Not a comment on attention disorders; don't present it as medical insight
cautions: Nearby verses are very bleak about the mind (a demon seizing a child, v.20); quote this one alone
A reader with diagnosed ADHD may find a 'scripture says your mind is a bird on meat' framing shaming; keep it general
speaks_to: starting many things and finishing none
not_for: someone already harshly self-critical about focus, unless paired with the 'train it gently' verse (2.9.33)
research_note: Only one classical commentary exists for this text (Anandabodhendra, 19th c.); its gloss is brief but changes the image (the child drops study for a toy).

verified_ref: Chandogya Upanishad 7.22.1 (the whole of section 22). Same in Jha (Shankara), Lokeswarananda and Müller (SBE 1, VII.22.1).
attribution_note: Sanatkumara to Narada; the final sentence ('Sir, I wish to understand happiness') is Narada's.
translation_note: Translation fine. The LINE overreaches: 'Understand the joy, and action follows' reverses the logic. The text says we act only when we expect happiness from it, and then says happiness itself needs investigating, which leads to 7.23: there is no happiness in the finite, only in the infinite (bhuma). Shankara also reads 'having found happiness' as anticipating a future good. Suggest: 'We only act when we expect some good from it. So ask what real happiness is.'
context: Sanatkumara is leading Narada up a ladder from name and speech through mind, will, thought, strength, food and so on. Just before: one serves only when one acts, and 'action' here, says Shankara, means restraining the senses and concentrating the mind (7.21). This verse: one acts only when one gets (expects) happiness. Next: the infinite alone is happiness; there is none in what is small (7.23).

key_terms.sense: gets, finds happiness (Shankara: anticipates it)
acts, does
is to be sought to be understood
happiness, well-being; next defined as bhuma, the infinite

core_teaching: People act only for some expected good, so the real question is what happiness actually is; the Upanishad's answer is that only the infinite, not anything limited, is happiness.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. Ganganatha Jha (1942)
commentaries.gist: One acts only once one has resolved that some good is to be gained; 'having obtained' really refers to the expected result. Lest anyone think the truth reveals itself automatically, the text adds that happiness must itself be investigated.

commentaries.who: Swami Lokeswarananda (Ramakrishna Mission), Chandogya Upanishad
commentaries.gist: Glosses it as: a person works when there is happiness in it and doesn't bother otherwise, so one must understand the true nature of that happiness. Links the preceding 'action' to disciplined practice.

practical_reading: If you can't get started, ask honestly what good you expect from the task. Often the block is that you don't see any. Finding the real reason it matters, not just forcing yourself, is what moves you.
misreadings: Not 'only do what feels fun'
Not a productivity hack; the passage is heading toward the infinite as the only real happiness
cautions: If paired with the next section (no happiness in the finite), it can sound dismissive of ordinary joys; frame gently
not_for: anhedonia from depression, where 'find the joy' can sound like blame

verified_ref: Katha Upanishad 1.2.2 (Adhyaya I, Valli II, verse 2). Same in Sitarama Sastri (Shankara), Vasu (Madhva) and Müller (SBE 15, I.2.2).
attribution_note: Yama to Nachiketa, correct.
translation_note: Good. 'Yoga-kshemat' (for getting and keeping) is read by Shankara as for the body's growth and upkeep, by Vasu's Madhva translation as acquiring and preserving objects, by Müller as greed and avarice. 'Samparitya' = going round them, examining from all sides.
context: Nachiketa has refused Yama's offers of wealth, long life and pleasures and insisted on knowing what happens after death. Yama now begins to teach: the good and the pleasant are two different things that pull a person different ways; whoever takes the good fares well, whoever chooses the pleasant misses the goal (1.2.1). After this verse he praises Nachiketa for rejecting 'the chain of wealth' in which many sink.

key_terms.sense: the good, what is truly beneficial
the pleasant, what is dear or gratifying
the wise, steady person
getting and keeping (possessions, security)

core_teaching: The good and the pleasant come to everyone mixed together; the wise person examines and separates them and chooses the good, while the careless grab the pleasant for gain and security.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. S. Sitarama Sastri
commentaries.gist: They arrive mixed and hard to tell apart; the wise sift them like a swan separating milk from water and choose the good; the dull take the pleasant (cattle, children) to sustain the body.

commentaries.who: Madhva tradition, tr. Srisa Chandra Vasu
commentaries.gist: Renders it: the good and the pleasant reach a soul through past causes; the wise examine and choose the good, while the ordinary person chooses pleasant objects and their acquisition and preservation.

practical_reading: When you want more, pause and ask whether this is good for you or just pleasant right now. Both feel similar in the moment; the work is telling them apart.
misreadings: Not 'pleasure is bad'; it ranks the two, it doesn't condemn enjoyment
'Getting and keeping' isn't a ban on financial security
cautions: Calls the other chooser 'manda' (dull, foolish); avoid labelling the reader
not_for: someone in poverty for whom 'getting and keeping' is survival

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 2.7.12 (Mumukshu-vyavahara-prakarana, sarga 7, 'establishing the primacy of effort'). Confirmed in the Nirnaya Sagar text with Tatparya-prakasha (1937); Mitra 1891, Mumukshu ch. VII v. 12.
attribution_note: Vasishtha to Rama, as stated.
translation_note: Close. 'Bring it down into good ones' is literal for 'avatarayet'; 'steer it back' in our line is fine. The verse is nearly repeated at 2.9.31, where Vasishtha addresses Rama directly ('turn your own mind').
context: In a chapter arguing that effort, not fate, governs life, Vasishtha says help comes from three sources (scripture, a teacher and one's own effort) and that all of them work through effort. Then he gives this verse as the essence of the scriptures. He goes on: teachers tell their students to pursue with effort what is excellent and lasting, and results come in proportion to effort.

key_terms.sense: (the mind) sunk into or absorbed in what is harmful
should bring it down into what is good
by deliberate effort
the summary of the meaning of all scriptures

core_teaching: When the mind is caught up in harmful things, deliberately redirect it toward good ones; this redirecting by effort is the heart of all teaching.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: Introduces the verse as the essential point, useful for the matter in hand, distilled from the scriptures just mentioned; the preceding verse is glossed as: worldly success comes by one's own effort, knowledge by effort plus scripture plus teacher.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Mumukshu ch. VII)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders it as the 'long and short of all the Sastras': diligence guards the mind from evil by applying it to what is good and right.

practical_reading: When you notice yourself sliding into a craving, comparison or unhelpful habit, don't just resist it; give the mind a better thing to do instead, and repeat.
misreadings: Not 'think only positive thoughts' or suppress hard feelings
Not a moral judgement that wanting things is bad; it is about where attention is placed
cautions: The same chapter says fate is a consolation only for weak minds (v.15) and that people go to hell for lack of effort (v.9); don't quote those to someone struggling
Effort framing can feel like blame for someone depressed or exhausted
not_for: someone in burnout or depression who needs rest more than effort

verified_ref: UNVERIFIED as Maha Upanishad 3.22: the Maha Upanishad texts we could reach (sanskritdocuments.org) are behind a bot check, so the chapter and verse number were not confirmed. VERIFIED: the same verse, almost word for word, is Yoga Vasishtha 1.17.8 (Nirnaya Sagar text with Tatparya-prakasha; Mokshopaya 1.16.8 on Sanskrit Wikisource), spoken by Rama in his lament on craving. Our wording ('muni-shreshtha', addressed to a sage) fits a Nidagha-to-Ribhu version of it; which text borrowed from which was not researched.
attribution_note: Nidagha to Ribhu is plausible for the Maha Upanishad but not confirmed here. In the Yoga Vasishtha the same verse is Rama's. Consider noting the parallel in the reading.
translation_note: Fair. Both YV commentators gloss the target as one's firm resolve or enthusiasm for good qualities: Anandabodhendra says craving cuts one's eagerness for the riches of virtues such as discernment and dispassion, and takes 'tantri' as the gut string of a lute (vina). So: 'whatever good quality I set my heart on, craving gnaws through it, as a mouse chews a lute-string.'
context: In the Yoga Vasishtha parallel (1.17), Rama describes craving: it dries him like the sun dries mud, dances like a demoness in the dark forest of his mind, drags him like a bull led by a nose-rope, and throws a net over people through attachment to children, friends and spouse. This verse comes early in that catalogue. In the Maha Upanishad version, the young Nidagha voices the same lament to his teacher Ribhu.

key_terms.sense: craving, thirst
the wealth or beauty of good qualities
I take refuge in, commit myself to
as a little mouse gnaws a string (lute-string)

core_teaching: Craving quietly undermines every good resolve or virtue we try to build, the way a mouse gnaws through a string.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha (on the Yoga Vasishtha parallel, 1.17.8)
commentaries.gist: Craving cuts through whatever eagerness one has for the wealth of virtues such as discernment and dispassion; the 'string' is a lute's gut string.

commentaries.who: Bhaskarakantha, Mokshopaya-tika (on the Mokshopaya parallel, 1.16.8; Sanskrit Wikisource)
commentaries.gist: Reads the verse with 'adhitastham' and glosses it as a resolve one has trained and made firm: even a firm commitment gets gnawed through.

practical_reading: If you keep making good resolutions and watching them fray, the problem may be the background wanting that nibbles at them, not your character. Notice the craving itself.
misreadings: Not 'you are weak-willed'
Not a condemnation of all desire; it targets restless craving
cautions: The surrounding lament is very bleak; quote this verse alone
Attribution and numbering need an editor's check before publishing the reference
not_for: someone already self-blaming about addiction, without a supportive frame
research_note: No Maha Upanishad commentary or reachable text found; the notes come from commentaries on the identical Yoga Vasishtha verse. Editor should confirm Maha Upanishad 3.22 against a printed edition (e.g. Adyar Library's Samanya Vedanta Upanishads).

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 1.12.15 (Vairagya-prakarana, sarga 12, 'first lament'). Confirmed in the Nirnaya Sagar text with Tatparya-prakasha (1937); Mitra 1891, Vairagya ch. XII v. 15.
attribution_note: Rama to Vishvamitra and Vasishtha. Strictly he is recalling the thoughts he had while on pilgrimage ('thus reflecting...', v.16).
translation_note: The last quarter ('kasya nama kim agatam') is read by Anandabodhendra as 'if it is false, let it be false; then what harm has come to anyone?' (no loss at all). Mitra similarly: no good or loss to anybody. Our 'what has anyone gained?' slightly shifts it from 'nothing is lost' to 'nothing is gained'. Suggest: 'If it is unreal, let it be unreal; what is lost to anyone?'
context: Asked by Vishvamitra why he is so low, Rama explains that after his pilgrimage he began to reflect: people are born to die and die to be born, pleasures are unstable, the world is built by the mind, and he has been chasing mirages like a deer. This verse caps that reflection. He then says such thinking made him lose all taste for the world, and asks the sages what this world really is.

key_terms.sense: what use to me is kingship, what use pleasures
who am I
unreal, false, illusory
what has come (to anyone): what is gained or lost

core_teaching: Rama questions the worth of everything he has and asks who he really is. The text treats this questioning as the healthy start of inquiry, not as despair to be fixed.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: Unpacks the questions: who am I, what is this world in essence and why has it come, is it all false or partly true? If false, let it be false: no one loses anything.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Vairagya ch. XII)
commentaries.gist: Places the verse in Rama's account of how pilgrimage reflections on birth, death and the mind's projections drained his interest in pleasures and led to questions about reality.

practical_reading: When nothing you own or do feels meaningful, the Yoga Vasishtha treats that emptiness as the doorway to a real question (who am I, what matters?) to be explored with a teacher, not a dead end.
misreadings: Not a recommendation to quit your job or responsibilities
Not nihilism: it is the question that opens the teaching, not its conclusion (our 'misuse' field already says this)
'Mithya' here is philosophical (not ultimately real), not 'pointless'
cautions: For a reader whose 'nothing matters' is depression, validating detachment could deepen it; pair with a grounding verse and gentle encouragement to talk to someone
Rama's lament runs for many chapters and is very bleak; don't quote other lines from it to a low reader
not_for: someone with signs of clinical depression or suicidal thoughts, unless paired with care and the answer verses

verified_ref: Ashtavakra Gita 16.2 (same number in Nityaswarupananda 1940 and Jalim Singh 1903).
attribution_note: Ashtavakra to Janaka, chapter 16 'Special instruction'.
translation_note: Our translation follows Nityaswarupananda: your mind will still yearn for That, beyond objects, where all desires are extinguished. Jalim Singh reads it the other way round: whether you enjoy, act or meditate, a mind free of all hope (through self-knowledge) will shine/be at peace, since only hope binds. Both readings are traditional; ours is fine, but the writer should not present the 'longing' as the only reading.
context: 16.1: you can recite and hear scriptures endlessly, but you won't rest in yourself without 'forgetting everything'. 16.2 is this verse. 16.3: everyone suffers from straining, and the lucky one who grasps this teaching finds peace. 16.4 praises the 'master idler' for whom even blinking is effort.

key_terms.sense: enjoyment, work or meditation
O wise one
with every desire or hope dropped
will long for intensely / will delight greatly

core_teaching: No activity, whether pleasure, work or even meditation, satisfies on its own; what the mind really wants is the state where wanting itself stops.

commentaries.who: Swami Nityaswarupananda, Astavakra Samhita (Advaita Ashrama, 1940), notes
commentaries.gist: Enjoyment, work and concentration all show the Self is not yet realised; none gives lasting satisfaction. The mind yearns for the Self, which lies beyond all quests and can't be realised until desire is gone.

commentaries.who: Rai Bahadur Babu Jalim Singh, Ashtavakra Gita bhasha-tika (Hindi, 1903)
commentaries.gist: Reads the verse positively: whatever you do, enjoy, act or meditate, your mind, emptied of hope by self-knowledge, will be at peace; actions done without hope do not bind, since hope is bondage.

practical_reading: If you've tried pleasure, productivity and even spiritual practice and still feel restless, the restlessness isn't a sign you picked the wrong activity; it points to wanting something none of them can give.
misreadings: Not 'nothing is worth doing'
Not anti-meditation; it says meditation as a goal-driven activity won't finish the job either
cautions: For someone flat or depressed, 'nothing satisfies' can confirm hopelessness; frame it as a pointer, not a verdict
Next verses (16.4 'master idler') need explanation if quoted
speaks_to: trying everything and still feeling empty
not_for: someone with clinical depression, unless paired with grounding and support

verified_ref: Surya Gita, ch. 3, verse 40 in the Mahamandal edition (second edition, 1967). That edition counts speaker lines ('rishaya ucuh', 'surya uvaca') as verses (four of them up to this point); our 3.36 matches once those are dropped. Wording matches.
attribution_note: Surya to the seven sages, correct (the edition's preface says the seven sages visited the sun's world and asked about action, worship and knowledge). This is one of the five sectarian 'Gitas' (Vishnu, Shambhu, Shakti, Surya, Dhisha) published by the Shri Bharat Dharma Mahamandal, Benares, c. 1916-1920; no independent manuscript tradition or classical commentary found (see vishnu_gita.1.60 entry). Present it as an early-20th-century devotional text, not an ancient one.
translation_note: Close. Strictly: 'when through experiencing pleasure and pain one has come to weariness (nirveda), one attains desirelessness, led by one's own discernment.' The edition's Hindi says the same: he becomes discerning and reaches freedom from desire.
context: The sages ask why even virtuous people are reborn. Surya answers that desire keeps regenerating the seeds of wrongdoing, and desire-driven good deeds earn rewards but don't purify the mind; without a pure mind there's no path to knowledge (vv. 35-38 in the 1967 numbering). This verse marks the turning point: weariness with pleasure and pain. After it he says that from then on, over several lives, one grows in the yoga of knowledge.

key_terms.sense: experiencing (tasting) pleasure and pain
weariness, disenchantment
freedom from craving, desirelessness
led by one's own discernment

core_teaching: Disenchantment that comes from having lived through enough highs and lows is not a failure; it is where real discernment and freedom from craving begin.

commentaries.who: Hindi translation in the Mahamandal edition (1967; no classical commentary exists)
commentaries.gist: Renders vv. 39-40: even with births driven by desire, scripture on liberation remains meaningful because selfless action can arise; after tasting pleasure and pain a person tires of them, becomes discerning and reaches desirelessness.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Sanskrit text, Surya Gita ch. 3)
commentaries.gist: The verse answers the sages' worry that the virtuous are still reborn: desire-tinged merit doesn't purify; disenchantment opens the path; knowledge then matures over several lives.

practical_reading: Feeling that the usual rewards no longer move you can be the beginning of a wiser relationship with them, if you let your own judgement, rather than numbness, lead.
misreadings: Not 'nothing matters'; nirveda here leads to discernment, not apathy
Not a claim that suffering is good for you
cautions: Late text; label accurately
Rebirth framing (over several lives) can feel distancing; leave it out of a reading for someone low
Can romanticise numbness; distinguish disenchantment from depression
not_for: someone whose flatness is depression and who needs care, not reframing
research_note: No commentary exists; the Hindi rendering and context come from the 1967 second edition (archive.org OCR). Prasang is null in our data.

verified_ref: Mundaka Upanishad 3.1.2 (Mundaka III, Khanda 1, verse 2). Same in Sitarama Sastri (Shankara), Vasu (Madhva) and Müller (SBE 15).
attribution_note: Angiras to Shaunaka, as stated.
translation_note: Mostly good. 'Jushtam' is read by Shankara as 'worshipped (by all)'; the Madhva translator's note calls the Lord 'ever-content', so our 'content lord' has support but is one reading. 'Anishaya' is 'through helplessness' for Shankara; Madhva reads it as the Lord's power that deludes the soul. Our line's 'the bird that eats' is from 3.1.1, fine as framing.
context: 3.1.1: two birds, close companions, sit on one tree; one eats the fruit, the other just watches. This verse: the person sunk on that tree grieves, confused by helplessness, until he sees the other, the Lord, and his greatness, and then sorrow leaves. 3.1.3 goes on: seeing the shining creator, the knower shakes off merit and demerit and reaches the highest sameness.

key_terms.sense: sunk, immersed (in the body and its concerns)
grieves through helplessness
bewildered, deluded
freed from sorrow

core_teaching: We suffer while we identify with the struggling self; seeing the calm witnessing presence (the Lord) and its greatness frees us from sorrow.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. S. Sitarama Sastri (1905)
commentaries.gist: Weighed down by ignorance and desire, the self takes the body as 'me' and grieves its losses (a son, a wife); taught by a compassionate teacher, it realises it is that Lord and crosses the ocean of grief.

commentaries.who: Madhva (Dvaita), tr. Srisa Chandra Vasu
commentaries.gist: The soul is deluded by the Lord's own free power and grieves; it is freed when it sees the ever-worshipped Lord as distinct from itself. The translator's note: discontent binds, contentment frees.

practical_reading: When you feel helpless and swamped, step back and notice the part of you that can watch the struggle without being lost in it. That steadier view eases the grief, even if circumstances don't change.
misreadings: Not 'your grief is just ignorance'
Advaita says you ARE the other bird, Dvaita says you see God as other; don't flatten these
cautions: Shankara's own examples of grief are a dead son and a dead wife; don't quote the bhashya to someone bereaved
Promises sorrow 'leaves'; for fresh grief, say 'eases' rather than 'ends'
speaks_to: being lost in one's own story
not_for: acute fresh grief, if presented as 'grief is delusion'

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 2.14.50 (Mumukshu-vyavahara-prakarana, sarga 14, 'on inquiry'). Confirmed in the Nirnaya Sagar text with Tatparya-prakasha (1937); Mitra 1891, Mumukshu ch. XIV v. 50.
attribution_note: Vasishtha to Rama, as stated.
translation_note: Good. 'Nyayena' (rightly) means by sound reasoning; the commentary says reasoning in line with scripture, sages and the teaching tradition.
context: This is the chapter on vichara, the second of the four gatekeepers to freedom. Vasishtha praises inquiry at length: an un-reflecting person suffers more than a sick man, and one should steady the mind by oneself through inquiry and carry it across the sea of delusion (v.49). Here he defines inquiry. He then says truth is known only through inquiry, truth brings rest in the self, and that rest ends sorrow.

key_terms.sense: who am I
the trouble or fault called worldly existence
reflection by sound reasoning
inquiry, investigation

core_teaching: Inquiry means honestly asking who you really are and how you came to be caught in this round of trouble, and reasoning it through. Vasishtha says this leads to knowledge, knowledge to inner rest, and rest to the end of sorrow.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: Two questions: am I the body and its parts or something different (the 'you' side), and how did worldly life arise on its ground (the 'that' side), reasoned in line with scripture, sages and the teaching tradition.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Mumukshu ch. XIV)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders it as reasoning within oneself about where the evil of worldliness began; surrounding verses say reason brings truth, truth brings peace, and peace dispels sorrow.

practical_reading: When life feels pointless, sit down with the questions directly: what in me is actually suffering, and how did I get into this pattern? Write them out rather than just feeling them.
misreadings: Not rumination or self-blame ('what is wrong with me?'); it is calm investigation
Not purely intellectual debate; the aim is inner rest
cautions: Nearby verses are harsh about those who don't inquire (better to be a frog in mud or a worm in filth, v.46; a stone heart, v.51); never quote those to a low reader
'Who am I?' can be destabilising for someone dissociating; keep the exercise concrete
not_for: acute crisis, where reflection can turn into rumination

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 1.10.19 (Vairagya-prakarana, sarga 10, 'Raghava's dejection'). Confirmed in the Nirnaya Sagar text with Tatparya-prakasha (1937); Mitra 1891, Vairagya ch. X v. 19.
attribution_note: Correct: the speaker is Rama's servant (rama-bhritya-janah), sent by the king to check on Rama, reporting to King Dasharatha.
translation_note: Good. Anandabodhendra glosses 'na udeti' as 'does not rejoice'. Mitra's 'cannot be excited to pleasantry' matches 'parihasa' (jokes, banter).
context: Dasharatha has noticed his son is changed since his pilgrimage and sends for news. The servant says Rama barely eats, avoids company, sees beautiful things with sorrowful eyes and calls everything unreal before falling silent (v.18). After this verse he says Rama seeks lonely places, lives like a wandering ascetic, and neither laughs, sings nor cries. Vishvamitra and Vasishtha then ask to hear Rama himself.

key_terms.sense: does not brighten at jokes
does not immerse himself in pleasures
does not stay with his tasks
clings only to silence

core_teaching: An outside observer's description of withdrawal: no joy in humour, pleasure or work, only silence. The text treats it seriously and responds with care and conversation, not scolding.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: Brief gloss only: 'does not rise' means he does not feel delight; the surrounding verses are explained as signs of a turning away from enjoyments.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Vairagya ch. X)
commentaries.gist: The attendant's whole report (vv. 9-28) lists the symptoms: little eating, avoiding company, calling all things unreal, solitude, no laughing, singing or crying; the king is distressed.

practical_reading: Losing the spark for jokes, pleasures and work is worth noticing and naming. In the story, the people around Rama noticed, worried, and brought help; it's okay to let someone do that for you.
misreadings: Not a portrait of spiritual achievement to imitate
Not 'withdrawal is wisdom'; the sages treat it as a state needing guidance
cautions: This describes classic signs of depression (anhedonia, withdrawal). Our 'misuse' field rightly says to talk to someone or a doctor if it lasts weeks; keep that
The sages' reading that Rama's state is dispassion, not illness, should not be applied to a real reader
not_for: anyone with suicidal thoughts, without a clear pointer to help

verified_ref: Chandogya Upanishad 7.1.3. Same in Jha (Shankara), Lokeswarananda and Müller (SBE 1, VII.1.3).
attribution_note: Narada speaks to Sanatkumara; the last sentence is Sanatkumara's reply. Our speaker 'Narada' is right for the main part.
translation_note: Good. 'Mantravit' = one who knows the texts (Shankara: only the words and the rituals they teach), versus 'atmavit', one who knows the self. 'Only name' (nama eva) is the first step of Sanatkumara's ladder, not a dismissal.
context: Narada asks Sanatkumara to teach him; asked what he knows, he lists the four Vedas, the epics, grammar, mathematics, logic, ethics, astronomy, the arts and more (7.1.2). Then comes this confession. Sanatkumara tells him all of it is name, to be honoured as Brahman, and leads him step by step upward to the infinite (bhuma), where happiness lies.

key_terms.sense: I know the texts, not the self
the knower of the self crosses sorrow
I grieve, I am in sorrow
it is only name

core_teaching: Knowing a great deal doesn't remove sorrow; Narada admits his learning hasn't touched the self, asks for help, and that honest admission begins the teaching.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. Ganganatha Jha (1942)
commentaries.gist: Narada knows only the words and rituals, not the self. His sorrow is the ache of not having fulfilled life's purpose. Even a sage needed a teacher; the story shows nothing but self-knowledge gives the highest good.

commentaries.who: Swami Lokeswarananda (Ramakrishna Mission), Chandogya Upanishad
commentaries.gist: Narada felt his scholarship was pointless without knowing the Self, like a donkey carrying sandalwood without enjoying its scent; with humility he asks to be taken across sorrow and helped to feel life's purpose fulfilled.

practical_reading: You can be accomplished and still feel empty, and saying so to someone wiser is the first step out. Narada, the most learned of all, did exactly that.
misreadings: Not anti-education; Sanatkumara honours each level as a step
Not 'your sadness means you're spiritually lacking'
cautions: Gentle and safe; the main risk is implying study was a waste for a reader who invested heavily in it
not_for: no strong contraindication

verified_ref: Vishnu Gita, ch. 1, verse 104 in the 1919 Bharat Dharma Mahamandal edition, which counts speaker lines as verses (our 1.60 is its 63; the gap grows as more speaker lines intervene). Wording matches.
attribution_note: Vishnu to the gods, correct. This is one of the five sectarian 'Gitas' (Vishnu, Shambhu, Shakti, Surya, Dhisha) published by the Shri Bharat Dharma Mahamandal, Benares, c. 1916-1920; no independent manuscript tradition or classical commentary found (see vishnu_gita.1.60 entry). Present it as an early-20th-century devotional text, not an ancient one. SOURCE NOTE: the verse closely reworks Bhartrihari's Vairagya-shataka 31 (GRETIL 3.31), which lists the same fears ('in honour the fear of humiliation, in virtue the fear of the wicked, in learning the fear of debaters... dispassion alone is fearless'). The Vishnu Gita splits it across vv. 102-105 of its own numbering.
translation_note: Good. 'Dinata' is abasement or humiliation; 'shakti' is power or capability (Bhartrihari has 'bala', strength, with fear of enemies); 'vadin' is a debating opponent. The edition's Hindi matches.
context: The gods asked how to be free of fear. Vishnu explains that attachment to perishable things born of ignorance breeds fear: the body fears age and death, wealth fears kings and thieves, youth fears old age, beauty fears decay, pleasure fears disease, family fears downfall (vv. 101-103 in the 1919 numbering). This verse adds honour, virtue, power and learning. The next verse says even heaven carries envy and the fear of falling, and only dispassion is fearless; then Vishnu recites Bhagavad Gita 2.13-15 to the gods.

key_terms.sense: in honour, the fear of humiliation
in virtue, the fear of the wicked
in power, the fear of critics
in learning, the fear of debaters

core_teaching: Every good thing we hold, even honour, virtue, power and learning, brings its own fear of losing it; only dispassion (vairagya) is free of fear.

commentaries.who: Hindi translation in the Mahamandal edition (1919; no classical commentary exists)
commentaries.gist: Lists the fears attached to each possession (honour fears abasement, virtue fears the wicked, power fears critics, learning fears debaters) and concludes that only the state of dispassion is truly without fear.

commentaries.who: Parallel: Bhartrihari, Vairagya-shataka 31 (GRETIL text)
commentaries.gist: The older source of the list: pleasure fears disease, family fears downfall, wealth fears kings, honour fears humiliation, learning fears debaters, virtue fears the wicked; everything on earth carries fear, and dispassion alone is fearless.

practical_reading: If you feel you're never good enough, notice that every achievement brings a new thing to defend. Security comes less from more achievement than from holding achievements more lightly.
misreadings: Not 'don't seek honour, skill or learning'
Not a claim that your fears are irrational; they are the natural shadow of what you value
cautions: Late text; label accurately, and consider crediting the idea to Bhartrihari
Surrounding verses list fears of death and family loss; don't quote them to a grieving reader
not_for: someone facing real threats (harassment, legal danger), where 'hold it lightly' would dismiss them

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 2.9.33 (Mumukshu-vyavahara-prakarana, sarga 9, 'on action'). Confirmed in the Nirnaya Sagar text with Tatparya-prakasha (1937); Mitra 1891, Mumukshu ch. IX v. 33.
attribution_note: Vasishtha to Rama, as stated.
translation_note: Translation is fair. Two flags for the line ('never by force'): (1) the verse says 'paurushena eva yatnena', by manly/strenuous effort; (2) the verse just before (2.9.32) says the mind is like a child and should be moved 'balat', forcibly, from bad to good. Anandabodhendra reconciles them: soothe and settle the child-mind quickly, then rein it in gradually, not suddenly by forcible suppression, citing Gita 6.25 ('slowly, slowly'). So 'gently, little by little' is right; 'never by force' overstates. Suggest: 'Look after your mind like a child: soothe it, steady it, little by little, with patient effort.'
context: Vasishtha argues that one's tendencies (vasanas) flow along a good and a bad channel and must be steered into the good one by effort. He says the mind is like a child. This verse gives the method. He goes on: whatever you have practised has become strong in you, so from today strengthen good tendencies; we become what we practise.

key_terms.sense: evenness, balance
soothing, coaxing
not abruptly, but slowly, little by little
the mind as a little child

core_teaching: Train your mind as you would raise a child: settle it, soothe it and guide it gradually with steady effort, rather than jolting it.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: Quickly bring the child-mind to its natural evenness by dropping the swings of attachment, soothe it, then restrain it gradually in the self; never abruptly by force, lest agitation break concentration. Cites Gita 6.25.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Mumukshu ch. IX)
commentaries.gist: Mitra renders it as training the mind like a child, slowly, by gentleness and indulgence rather than force and hurry; next verses urge directing habits toward good from now on.

practical_reading: Treat your own mind the way a good parent treats a child: no shaming, small steps, consistent gentle redirection. Self-improvement works better as patient training than as self-punishment.
misreadings: Not 'no effort needed': the verse insists on steady effort
Not permission to indulge every impulse; gentleness is a method, not a lack of direction
cautions: The very next verses say 'we become what we practise'; fine, but avoid implying a reader's struggles are their own bad habits
not_for: no strong contraindication
research_note: Mitra's rendering of v.32 ('must not be employed by force') differs from the Sanskrit printed in the Nirnaya Sagar edition ('chalayed balat', move it forcibly); Mitra seems to read v.32 in the light of v.33.

verified_ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 4.4.5 (last part of the paragraph). Same in Madhavananda (Shankara) and Müller (SBE 15, IV.4.5).
attribution_note: Yajnavalkya to King Janaka, correct. Within the verse this is introduced as what 'others say' (atho khalv ahuh), a view Yajnavalkya cites; Shankara explains it as other authorities holding that desire alone is the root.
translation_note: Last clause: 'tad abhisampadyate' means 'that (result) he attains/reaps' (Madhavananda: 'it attains'; Müller: 'that he will reap'), not 'that he becomes'. The 'becomes' idea is in the verse's first half ('as one acts, so one becomes'). Our line 'as your deeds, so you become' blends the two; acceptable for a reading, but the precise sense is reaping results.
context: Yajnavalkya is explaining to Janaka what happens at death: the self leaves the body like a caterpillar moving to the next blade of grass and makes a new form like a goldsmith reshaping gold. In this verse he says the self takes on whatever it identifies with, and as it acts, so it becomes; then cites the view that a person is made of desire. Next (4.4.6) he says the one attached goes to the fruits of his deeds and returns, while the one free of desire, being Brahman, goes to Brahman.

key_terms.sense: made of desire
as one's desire is
will, resolve, determination
action, deed
attains, reaps (the result)

core_teaching: Desire shapes resolve, resolve shapes action, and action shapes what one attains; the Upanishad uses this to explain rebirth and points beyond it to freedom from desire.

commentaries.who: Shankara (Advaita), tr. Swami Madhavananda
commentaries.gist: A slight longing, if unchecked, firms into resolve, which leads to action and its results; so desire is the root of transmigration. Without desire, actions bear no binding fruit.

commentaries.who: Max Müller tr., SBE 15 (1884)
commentaries.gist: Renders the chain as desire to will, will to deed, deed to what one reaps; the next paragraph contrasts the desiring man, who returns to this world of action, with the desireless one who goes to Brahman.

practical_reading: To keep a resolve, look upstream at what you actually want. Teachers use this verse to say that clarifying desire is the first step of any lasting change.
misreadings: Not a self-help manifestation promise ('want it and you'll get it')
Not a celebration of desire; the passage's goal is freedom from it
cautions: The passage is about death and rebirth; avoid that frame for grieving readers
'You become your deeds' can feel like blame for someone who failed a resolve
not_for: someone in shame over a relapse, without a gentler frame
research_note: Swami Krishnananda's commentary site shows a bot check, so it was not used.

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 2.7.17 (Mumukshu-vyavahara-prakarana, sarga 7, 'establishing the primacy of effort'). Confirmed in the Nirnaya Sagar text with Tatparya-prakasha (1937); Mitra 1891, Mumukshu ch. VII v. 17.
attribution_note: Vasishtha to Rama, as stated.
translation_note: Small embellishment: 'vakta vakti na chavakta' is 'the speaker speaks, not the non-speaker'. 'Is heard' adds a result the verse doesn't state. Suggest 'the one who speaks gets said what he means; the silent one doesn't', or simply 'the speaker speaks'.
context: Vasishtha is building his case that effort, not fate, brings results. Just before, he says effort's results are seen every day, as in people who travel far to earn (v.16), and fate is a comfort only for weak minds (v.15). After this he says the wise escape hard straits by effort while the fatalist sits idle, and each gets fruit according to how he strives.

key_terms.sense: the one who eats is satisfied
the one who walks gets somewhere
human effort bears fruit

core_teaching: Results come from doing. Eating fills you, walking gets you there; waiting for fate does neither.

commentaries.who: Anandabodhendra Sarasvati, Tatparya-prakasha
commentaries.gist: Very brief: the verse completes the previous point, that the fruit of effort is plainly 'seen to be fruitful' in everyday life.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Mumukshu ch. VII)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: the eater is sated, the walker proceeds, the speaker is a speaker; action makes the man. Next verses: the wise escape difficulties by exertion, while the idle fatalist gets nothing.

practical_reading: When a resolve stalls, take one concrete step today; the verse's examples are tiny physical acts, not grand plans.
misreadings: Not 'success is purely your own doing' or contempt for those facing bad luck
Not a call to overwork
cautions: The chapter is scornful of fatalists and the weak-minded (v.15, v.18); keep quotes to this verse
For someone whose effort is blocked by illness, poverty or others, 'effort always bears fruit' can sting
not_for: someone exhausted, ill or facing obstacles beyond their control

verified_ref: Yoga Vasishtha 1.12.22 (Vairagya-prakarana, sarga 12, 'first lament'). Confirmed on Sanskrit Wikisource (Nirnaya Sagar text) and Mitra 1891, Vairagya ch. XII v. 22. The page with this verse is illegible in the archive.org OCR of the Tatparya-prakasha, so its commentary was not read.
attribution_note: Rama to Vishvamitra and Vasishtha, as stated.
translation_note: Good. 'Nija-loka' is 'my own people' (family, court), as Mitra also takes it. 'Nirandhra' means packed with no gap: the stones of sorrow leave no opening.
context: Late in Rama's first lament he says the thought of how to end sorrow burns him like fire inside a hollow tree (v.21). In this verse he admits he holds back tears because of what his people would think. The next verse says his face shows nothing, his crying is tearless, and only the discernment in his heart sees it when he is alone. He ends by saying his mind finds no rest, like a chained wild elephant.

key_terms.sense: the stones of life's sorrows
with a heart packed solid, no gap left
out of fear of my own people
I do not weep with falling tears

core_teaching: Rama admits the hidden weight of sorrow he carries and that he hides it out of fear of how his own people would see him. Saying this aloud to the sages is where his help begins.

commentaries.who: Context of the chapter (Mitra tr. 1891, Vairagya ch. XII)
commentaries.gist: Mitra: worldly misery sits on his heart like a rock and stops his breath; he wants to weep but holds back for fear of his people; his tearless grief is known only to his own consciousness in solitude.

commentaries.who: Surrounding text (Sanskrit, Vairagya 12.21-27)
commentaries.gist: Before: anxiety burns him like fire in a hollow tree. After: tearless, blank-faced crying seen only in solitude; prosperity deludes; his mind finds no rest, like a chained elephant.

practical_reading: Many people carry grief or strain silently because they fear looking weak to family or colleagues. Noticing that you're holding back, and finding one safe person to tell, is the first relief.
misreadings: Not praise for keeping a stiff upper lip (our 'misuse' field says this well)
Not a statement that crying is shameful
cautions: Rama's lament is unrelievedly bleak; follow with something that opens a way forward
speaks_to: men or eldest children expected not to cry
not_for: no strong contraindication
research_note: No commentary read for this verse: the Tatparya-prakasha page is missing from the OCR. Both entries are context, not commentary.
